The book is the founding text of the Lydian Chromatic Concept (LCC), or Lydian Chromatic Theory (LCT). Russell's work postulates that all music is based on the tonal gravity of the [Lydian mode](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lydian_mode "Lydian mode"). ## Deriving Lydian \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Lydian_Chromatic_Concept_of_Tonal_Organization&action=edit§ion=1 "Edit section: Deriving Lydian")\] Russell believed that [dominant function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominant_function "Dominant function") is the driving force behind all harmonic motion. Russell focuses on the Lydian mode because it can be built with fifths. For instance, to construct a C Lydian scale one could list the first seven tones on the [circle of fifths](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Circle_of_fifths "Circle of fifths") starting with C, the desired Lydian Tonic. This process would yield C, G, D, A, E, B, F♯. If these tones are voiced in the space of an octave, they form the Lydian mode; specifically, C Lydian (C, D, E, F♯, G, A, B).[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lydian_Chromatic_Concept_of_Tonal_Organization#cite_note-Deriving_Lydian_with_Fifths-2) Additionally, Russell observed, when these tones are voiced in thirds they form the preferred form of a major 13 (#11) chord.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lydian_Chromatic_Concept_of_Tonal_Organization#cite_note-13th_chord_derivation-3) ## The Lydian Chromatic Scale \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Lydian_Chromatic_Concept_of_Tonal_Organization&action=edit§ion=2 "Edit section: The Lydian Chromatic Scale")\] Russell builds a prototype chromatic scale starting on the Lydian Tonic by stacking fifths, skipping the interval between the seventh and eighth tones, and placing the skipped tone at the end for having the lowest level of tonal gravity. Using C as the Lydian Tonic yields the following 12-note scale with [enharmonic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enharmonic "Enharmonic") respellings: C, G, D, A, E, B, F♯, G♯, E♭ (D♯), B♭ (A♯), F (E♯), D♭ (C♯). Thus the Lydian Chromatic Scale and all its derivatives contain only [Pythagorean intervals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pythagorean_interval "Pythagorean interval").[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lydian_Chromatic_Concept_of_Tonal_Organization#cite_note-4) ## Tonal gravity \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Lydian_Chromatic_Concept_of_Tonal_Organization&action=edit§ion=3 "Edit section: Tonal gravity")\] Russell posited that tonal gravity emanates from the first seven tones of the Lydian mode. As the player ventures further from the Lydian tonic however (and further up the circle of fifths), the tonal gravity shifts. For example, if notes further up the circle of fifths (e.g. ♯2/♭3) are used, the tonal gravity is probably shifting.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lydian_Chromatic_Concept_of_Tonal_Organization#cite_note-Tonal_gravity-5) ## Influence \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Lydian_Chromatic_Concept_of_Tonal_Organization&action=edit§ion=4 "Edit section: Influence")\] Russell's theory has had far-reaching effect especially in the realm of modal jazz. [Art Farmer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_Farmer "Art Farmer") said that it "opens the door to countless means of melodic expression"[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lydian_Chromatic_Concept_of_Tonal_Organization#cite_note-6) and critic [Joachim-Ernst Berendt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joachim-Ernst_Berendt "Joachim-Ernst Berendt") described it as "the first work deriving a theory of jazz harmony from the immanent laws of jazz" and as "the pathbreaker for [Miles Davis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis "Miles Davis")'s and [John Coltrane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Coltrane "John Coltrane")'s 'modality'".[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lydian_Chromatic_Concept_of_Tonal_Organization#cite_note-7) [Bill Evans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans "Bill Evans") and Miles Davis used the theory[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lydian_Chromatic_Concept_of_Tonal_Organization#cite_note-Russell's_relationship_with_Evans-8)[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lydian_Chromatic_Concept_of_Tonal_Organization#cite_note-Impact_of_LCC-9) to record modal jazz such as the album _[Kind of Blue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kind_of_Blue "Kind of Blue")_. John Coltrane's modal jazz is usually analyzed using Russell's method.[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lydian_Chromatic_Concept_of_Tonal_Organization#cite_note-Modal_Trane-10) In arguably his most famous piece, " [Giant Steps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giant_Steps_(composition) "Giant Steps (composition)")," Coltrane can be heard traveling through a succession of three parent Lydian Chromatic scales: C Lydian, A♭ Lydian, and E Lydian.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lydian_Chromatic_Concept_of_Tonal_Organization#cite_note-11) Additionally, many conservatories teach Russell's theory to varying degrees.[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lydian_Chromatic_Concept_of_Tonal_Organization#cite_note-Impact_of_LCC2-12)[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lydian_Chromatic_Concept_of_Tonal_Organization#cite_note-Teaching_LCC-13) ## See also \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Lydian_Chromatic_Concept_of_Tonal_Organization&action=edit§ion=5 "Edit section: See also")\] - - gamelan | Musical artist **Donald Eugene Cherry** (November 18, 1936 – October 19, 1995)[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter)#cite_note-1) was an American jazz trumpeter, bandleader, and multi-instrumentalist. Beginning in the late 1950s, he had a long tenure performing in the bands of saxophonist [Ornette Coleman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornette_Coleman "Ornette Coleman"), including on the pioneering [free jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_jazz "Free jazz") albums _[The Shape of Jazz to Come](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Shape_of_Jazz_to_Come "The Shape of Jazz to Come")_ (1959) and _[Free Jazz: A Collective Improvisation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_Jazz:_A_Collective_Improvisation "Free Jazz: A Collective Improvisation")_ (1961). Cherry also collaborated separately with musicians including [John Coltrane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Coltrane "John Coltrane"), [Charlie Haden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charlie_Haden "Charlie Haden"), [Sun Ra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sun_Ra "Sun Ra"), [Ed Blackwell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Blackwell "Ed Blackwell"), the [New York Contemporary Five](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_Contemporary_Five "New York Contemporary Five"), and [Albert Ayler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_Ayler "Albert Ayler"). Cherry released his debut album as bandleader, _[Complete Communion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Complete_Communion "Complete Communion")_, in 1966. In the 1970s, he became a pioneer in [world fusion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_music "World music"), with his work drawing on African, Middle Eastern, and [Hindustani](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hindustani_classical_music "Hindustani classical music") music, as heard on the 1975 release _[Brown Rice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brown_Rice_(album) "Brown Rice (album)")_. He was a member of the [ECM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ECM_Records "ECM Records") group [Codona](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Codona "Codona"), along with percussionist [Naná Vasconcelos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nan%C3%A1_Vasconcelos "Naná Vasconcelos") and sitar and tabla player [Collin Walcott](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Collin_Walcott "Collin Walcott").[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter)#cite_note-2) Chris Kelsey of [AllMusic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AllMusic "AllMusic") called Cherry "one of the most influential jazz musicians of the late 20th century."[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter)#cite_note-3) ## Early life Cherry was born in [Oklahoma City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oklahoma_City "Oklahoma City"), [Oklahoma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oklahoma "Oklahoma"), to a mother of [Choctaw](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Choctaw "Choctaw") descent and an [African-American](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/African_Americans "African Americans") father.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter)#cite_note-4) His mother and grandmother played piano and his father played trumpet.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter)#cite_note-atc1995-5) His father owned Oklahoma City's Cherry Blossom Club, which hosted performances by jazz musicians [Charlie Christian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charlie_Christian "Charlie Christian") and [Fletcher Henderson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fletcher_Henderson "Fletcher Henderson").[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter)#cite_note-biojazz-6) In 1940, Cherry moved with his family to the [Watts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Watts,_Los_Angeles "Watts, Los Angeles") neighborhood of [Los Angeles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles "Los Angeles"), where his father tended bar at the Plantation Club on [Central Avenue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Avenue_(Los_Angeles) "Central Avenue (Los Angeles)"), at the time the center of a vibrant jazz scene.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter)#cite_note-biojazz-6)[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter)#cite_note-cadence-7)[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter)#cite_note-carr-8) Cherry recalled skipping school at [Fremont High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_C._Fremont_High_School "John C. Fremont High School") in order to play with the [swing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swing_music "Swing music") band at [Jefferson High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jefferson_High_School_(Los_Angeles) "Jefferson High School (Los Angeles)").[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter)#cite_note-cadence-7) This resulted in his transfer to Jacob Riis High School, a [reform school](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reform_school "Reform school"),[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter)#cite_note-cadence-7) where he met drummer [Billy Higgins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billy_Higgins "Billy Higgins").[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter)#cite_note-voce1995-9)[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter)#cite_note-crouch-10) ## Career [... middle omitted — see footer ...] | Albums | - _[Mudfoot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mudfoot "Mudfoot")_ (1986)

[Collin Walcott](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Collin_Walcott "Collin Walcott") | **Codona** was a [free jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_jazz "Free jazz") and [world fusion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_fusion "World fusion") group which released three self-titled albums on the [ECM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ECM_(record_label) "ECM (record label)") label in 1979, 1981 and 1983. The trio consisted of [multi-instrumentalists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multi-instrumentalist "Multi-instrumentalist") [Don Cherry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(jazz) "Don Cherry (jazz)"), [Collin Walcott](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Collin_Walcott "Collin Walcott"), and [Nana Vasconcelos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nana_Vasconcelos "Nana Vasconcelos"). The name of the group was derived from the first two letters of the musicians' first names (COllin, DOn, NAna).[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Codona#cite_note-1) The members of the group declared that their goal was "to be open and incorporate all we know, without turning the whole world into milk toast - still encouraging the survival of the traditions".[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Codona#cite_note-2) Critic [Robert Palmer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Palmer_(American_writer) "Robert Palmer (American writer)") stated that the group's "self-appointed mission is to fuse African, Indian and other music traditions in the heat of improvisation".[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Codona#cite_note-3) The authors of [The Penguin Guide to Jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Penguin_Guide_to_Jazz "The Penguin Guide to Jazz") on CD called the group's debut album "one of the iconic episodes in so-called (but never better called) 'world music'", and stated: "Any tendency to regard Codona's music... as floating impressionism is sheer prejudice, for all these performances are deeply rooted in modern jazz (Coltrane's harmonies and rhythms, Ornette Coleman's melodic and rhythmic primitivism) and in another great and related improvisational tradition from Brazil."[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Codona#cite_note-4) ## Background The musicians had crossed paths on a number of occasions prior to the formation of the group in 1977.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Codona#cite_note-5) Vasconcelos appeared on Cherry's album _[Organic Music Society](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Organic_Music_Society "Organic Music Society")_, recorded and released in 1972,[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Codona#cite_note-6) while Walcott played on Cherry's _[Hear & Now](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hear_&_Now_(Don_Cherry_album) "Hear & Now (Don Cherry album)")_, recorded in 1976 and released in 1977.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Codona#cite_note-7) Cherry also appeared on Walcott's _[Grazing Dreams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grazing_Dreams "Grazing Dreams")_, recorded and released in 1977,[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Codona#cite_note-8) while both Walcott and Vasconcelos played on [Egberto Gismonti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Egberto_Gismonti "Egberto Gismonti")'s _[Sol do Meio Dia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sol_do_Meio_Dia "Sol do Meio Dia")_, recorded in 1977 and released in 1978.[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Codona#cite_note-9) The members' involvement with Codona overlapped with their participation in other projects, Cherry with [Old and New Dreams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_and_New_Dreams "Old and New Dreams"), Walcott with [Oregon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oregon_(band) "Oregon (band)"), and Vasconcelos with [Pat Metheny](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pat_Metheny "Pat Metheny"), [Milton Nascimento](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milton_Nascimento "Milton Nascimento"), [Jan Garbarek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jan_Garbarek "Jan Garbarek"), [Jon Hassell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jon_Hassell "Jon Hassell"), and others. Although the group was conceived as a leaderless trio, Walcott was the organizer and primary composer.[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Codona#cite_note-10)[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Codona#cite_note-11) Codona was noted for its use of a broad range of instrumentation.[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Codona#cite_note-kelman-12) While Cherry was primarily known as a trumpet and cornet player, he also performed on various [flutes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flute "Flute"), [organ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Organ_(music) "Organ (music)"), [melodica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Melodica "Melodica"), and the [Malian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mali "Mali") doussn’gouni.[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Codona#cite_note-grillo-13) Walcott played [sitar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sitar "Sitar"), [tabla](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tabla "Tabla"), [hammered dulcimer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hammered_dulcimer "Hammered dulcimer"), [sanza](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mbira "Mbira"), and [timpani](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timpani "Timpani"), while Vasconcelos performed on [berimbau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berimbau "Berimbau"), [cuica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cuica "Cuica"), [talking drum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Talking_drum "Talking drum"), and a variety of [percussion instruments](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Percussion_instrument "Percussion instrument").[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Codona#cite_note-grillo-13) In addition, all three musicians sang.[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Codona#cite_note-grillo-13) The group was also known for its unusual arrangements, an example being "Colemanwonder", a medley of two [Ornette Coleman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornette_Coleman "Ornette Coleman") tunes combined with [Stevie Wonder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stevie_Wonder "Stevie Wonder")'s " [Sir Duke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sir_Duke "Sir Duke")", performed on trumpet, sitar, cuica, and percussion, and appearing on the group's [debut album](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Codona_(album) "Codona (album)").[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Codona#cite_note-kelman-12) The group disbanded following Walcott's death in a traffic accident in [East Germany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Germany "East Germany") in 1984. ## Discography - 1979: _[Codona](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Codona_(album) "Codona (album)")_ (ECM Released: 1974 | | | _**Head Hunters**_ is the twelfth [studio album](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Studio_album "Studio album") by American pianist, keyboardist and composer [Herbie Hancock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbie_Hancock "Herbie Hancock"), released October 26, 1973, on [Columbia Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbia_Records "Columbia Records"). Recording sessions for the album took place in the evening at [Wally Heider Studios](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wally_Heider_Studios "Wally Heider Studios") and [Different Fur Trading Co.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Different_Fur "Different Fur") in [San Francisco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Francisco "San Francisco"), [California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California "California"). Hancock is featured with woodwind player [Bennie Maupin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bennie_Maupin "Bennie Maupin") from his previous "Mwandishi" sextet and three new collaborators – bassist [Paul Jackson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Jackson_(bassist) "Paul Jackson (bassist)"), percussionist [Bill Summers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Summers_(musician) "Bill Summers (musician)"), and drummer [Harvey Mason](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvey_Mason "Harvey Mason"). The latter group of collaborators, which would go on to be known as [the Headhunters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Headhunters "The Headhunters"), also played on Hancock's subsequent studio album _[Thrust](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thrust_(album) "Thrust (album)")_ (1974). All of the musicians (with the exception of Mason) play multiple instruments on the album. The album was a commercial and artistic breakthrough for Hancock, crossing over to [funk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Funk "Funk") and [rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rock_music "Rock music") audiences and bringing [jazz-funk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz-funk "Jazz-funk") and [jazz fusion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_fusion "Jazz fusion") to mainstream attention, peaking at number 13 on the [_Billboard_ 200](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_200 "Billboard 200"). Today the album is regarded as a landmark of fusion and has influenced artists in numerous other genres. In 2008, the [Library of Congress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Library_of_Congress "Library of Congress") inducted it into the [National Recording Registry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Recording_Registry "National Recording Registry") for being "culturally, historically or aesthetically important".[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Head_Hunters#cite_note-3) ## Background and recording _Head Hunters_ followed three experimental albums by Hancock's "Mwandishi" sextet: _[Mwandishi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mwandishi "Mwandishi")_, _[Crossings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crossings_(Herbie_Hancock_album) "Crossings (Herbie Hancock album)")_, and _[Sextant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sextant_(album) "Sextant (album)")_, released between 1971 and 1973. He later reflected on moving away from this style: > I began to feel that I had been spending so much time exploring the upper atmosphere of music and the more ethereal kind of far-out spacey stuff. Now there was this need to take some more of the earth and to feel a little more tethered; a connection to the earth. ... I was beginning to feel that we (the sextet) were playing this heavy kind of music, and I was tired of everything being heavy. I wanted to play something lighter. —Hancock's sleeve notes: 1997 CD reissue For the new album, Hancock assembled a new band, [the Headhunters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Headhunters "The Headhunters"), of whom only woodwind player [Bennie Maupin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bennie_Maupin "Bennie Maupin") had been a member of the "Mwandishi" sextet. Hancock handled all synthesizer parts himself, having shared these duties with [Patrick Gleeson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_Gleeson "Patrick Gleeson") on _Crossings_ and _Sextant,_ and decided against the use of guitar altogether in favor of the Hohner [Clavinet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clavinet "Clavinet"), one of the defining sounds on the album. The new band featured a tight [rhythm section](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhythm_section "Rhythm section") composed of [Paul Jackson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Jackson_(bassist) "Paul Jackson (bassist)") (bass guitar) and [Harvey Mason](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvey_Mason "Harvey Mason") (drums), creating a relaxed [funk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Funk "Funk") sensibility that gave it an appeal to a wider audience. | Professional ratings _**Mwandishi**_ is the ninth studio album by American [jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz "Jazz") pianist [Herbie Hancock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbie_Hancock "Herbie Hancock"), released in March 1971. It is the first album to officially feature Hancock’s ‘Mwandishi’ sextet, consisting of reed player [Bennie Maupin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bennie_Maupin "Bennie Maupin"), trumpeter [Eddie Henderson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddie_Henderson_(musician) "Eddie Henderson (musician)"), trombonist [Julian Priester](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julian_Priester "Julian Priester"), bassist [Buster Williams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buster_Williams "Buster Williams"), and drummer [Billy Hart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billy_Hart "Billy Hart"). ## Background \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Mwandishi&action=edit§ion=1 "Edit section: Background")\] This album is one of Hancock's first departures from the traditional idioms of jazz, as well as the beginning of an original and creative style which eventually appealed to a wider audience. In addition, _Mwandishi_ was Hancock's attempt at continuing the musical principles and styles he explored in his previous experiences with [Miles Davis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis "Miles Davis") (on the album _[In A Silent Way](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/In_A_Silent_Way "In A Silent Way")_, for instance). Hancock's previous explorations of [jazz fusion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_fusion "Jazz fusion") included _[Fat Albert Rotunda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fat_Albert_Rotunda "Fat Albert Rotunda")_, an album related to the TV special ‘’ [Hey, Hey, Hey, It's Fat Albert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hey,_Hey,_Hey,_It's_Fat_Albert "Hey, Hey, Hey, It's Fat Albert")’’. _Mwandishi_ was recorded at [Wally Heider Studios](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wally_Heider_Studios "Wally Heider Studios") Studio C, San Francisco, in January 1971. The recording incorporated progressive notions of funk, jazz, and rock. The tracks on _Mwandishi_ include "Ostinato," the [time signature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time_signature "Time signature") of which is **15** **8**, "You'll Know When You Get There," and "Wandering Spirit Song." "Wandering Spirit Song" features Hancock's extensive use of tension and release, in which he builds the tension of the song by crescendos and an increasing number of musical voices, and then releases the tension with long held chords on his [synthesizer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Synthesizer "Synthesizer"). - [space rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_rock "Space rock") | **Progressive rock** (shortened to **prog rock** or simply **prog**) is a broad [genre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Music_genre "Music genre") of [rock music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rock_music "Rock music")[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMartin199871%E2%80%9375-9) that primarily developed in the United States and United Kingdom through the mid- to late 1960s. Initially termed " [progressive pop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_pop "Progressive pop")", the style emerged from [psychedelic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Psychedelic_music "Psychedelic music") bands who abandoned standard [pop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pop_music "Pop music") or [rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rock_music "Rock music") traditions in favour of [instrumental](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Instrumentation_(music) "Instrumentation (music)") and [compositional](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Composition_(music) "Composition (music)") techniques more commonly associated with [jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz "Jazz"), [folk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Folk_music "Folk music"), or [classical music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Classical_music "Classical music"), while retaining the instrumentation typical of rock music. Additional elements contributed to its " [progressive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_music "Progressive music")" label: lyrics were more poetic, technology was harnessed for new sounds, music approached the condition of " [art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_music "Art music")", and the studio, rather than the stage, [became the focus of musical activity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Recording_studio_as_an_instrument "Recording studio as an instrument"), which often involved creating music for listening rather than dancing. Progressive rock includes a fusion of styles, approaches and genres, and tends to be diverse and [eclectic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eclecticism_in_music "Eclecticism in music"). Progressive rock is often associated with long solos, extended pieces, fantastic lyrics, grandiose stage sets and costumes, and an obsessive dedication to technical skill and [virtuosity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virtuoso "Virtuoso"). While the genre is often cited for its merging of [high culture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/High_culture "High culture") and [low culture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Low_culture "Low culture"), few artists incorporated Western classical themes in their work to a significant degree, with only a minority of groups ( [Emerson, Lake & Palmer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emerson,_Lake_&_Palmer "Emerson, Lake & Palmer"), [Renaissance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Renaissance_(band) "Renaissance (band)"), [Ekseption](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ekseption "Ekseption"), etc.) directly emulating or referencing classical music. (m.1970)​ | Musical artist **Keith Graham Tippetts** (25 August 1947 – 14 June 2020),[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Tippett#cite_note-guardian-1) known professionally as **Keith Tippett**, was a British [jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz "Jazz") pianist and composer. According to [AllMusic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AllMusic "AllMusic"), Tippett's career "...spanned jazz-rock, [progressive rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock "Progressive rock"), improvised and contemporary music, as well as modern jazz for more than half-a-century". He held "an unparallelled place in British contemporary music,"[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Tippett#cite_note-Eder-2) and was known for "his unique approach to improvisation".[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Tippett#cite_note-guardian-1) Tippett appeared and recorded in many settings, including a duet with [Stan Tracey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stan_Tracey "Stan Tracey"), duets with his wife [Julie Tippetts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julie_Tippetts "Julie Tippetts") (née Driscoll), solo performances, and as a bandleader.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Tippett#cite_note-guy-3) ## Early life Born in [Southmead](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southmead "Southmead"), [Bristol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol "Bristol"), England,[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Tippett#cite_note-LarkinJazz-4) Tippett was the son of an English father who was a policeman and an Irish mother named Kitty. He wrote music dedicated to her after she died. He was the oldest of three siblings and went to Greenway Secondary Modern school in Southmead. As a child he played piano, church organ, cornet, and tenor horn.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Tippett#cite_note-Eder-2) At fourteen he formed his first band, KT Trad Lads, with school friends Richard Murch, Mike Milton, Terry Pratt, and Bob Chard, and Eric Condell performing traditional jazz. He formed a modern jazz trio in Bristol and played regularly at the Dugout Club in Park Row, Bristol. ## Music career In 1967, Tippett moved to London to pursue a career in music, taking menial jobs while performing in jazz clubs.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Tippett#cite_note-Eder-2) With a scholarship he attended the Barry Summer School Jazz Course in Wales, where he met [Elton Dean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elton_Dean "Elton Dean"), [Nick Evans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Evans_(trombonist) "Nick Evans (trombonist)"), and [Marc Charig](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marc_Charig "Marc Charig") and with them started a band.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Tippett#cite_note-Eder-2) The Keith Tippett Sextet was hired for a residency at the [100 Club](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/100_Club "100 Club") in Oxford Street,[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Tippett#cite_note-LarkinJazz-4) leading to a contract with Polydor, which released their first two albums, _You Are There... I Am Here_ (1970) and _Dedicated to You, but You Weren't Listening_ (1971).[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Tippett#cite_note-Eder-2) After leaving Vertigo, Tippett formed [Centipede](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Centipede_(band) "Centipede (band)"), a 50-piece band that included his wife [Julie Driscoll](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julie_Driscoll "Julie Driscoll"), and brought together much of a generation of young British jazz and rock musicians.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Tippett#cite_note-Eder-2) As well as performing some concerts (limited economically by the size of the band), they recorded one double-album, _[Septober Energy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Septober_Energy "Septober Energy")_, a Tippett composition, which was released on the [RCA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RCA_Records "RCA Records") label in 1971. Despite substantial publicity, the album failed to sell in sufficient numbers to justify the expense of maintaining the project.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Tippett#cite_note-Eder-2) In early 1970, Tippett was part of a temporary [King Crimson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Crimson "King Crimson") line-up for the recording of their second album _[In the Wake of Poseidon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/In_the_Wake_of_Poseidon "In the Wake of Poseidon")_.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Tippett#cite_note-5)[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Tippett#cite_note-6)[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Tippett#cite_note-7) He also contributed as a session musician to the band's subsequent two albums _[Lizard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lizard_(album) "Lizard (album)")_ later in 1970 and _[Islands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islands_(King_Crimson_album) "Islands (King Crimson album)")_ in 1971. For his next album as a leader, _Blueprint_ (1972),[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Tippett#cite_note-LarkinJazz-4) he used a smaller group comprising himself and Julie Tippetts with bassist [Roy Babbington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roy_Babbington "Roy Babbington") and drummer Frank Perry. The band then expanded slightly to become Ovary Lodge,[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Tippett#cite_note-LarkinJazz-4) who recorded two albums, one for RCA and a second for the Ogun label. Tippett and his band also recorded in the 1970s for [Giorgio Gomelsky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giorgio_Gomelsky "Giorgio Gomelsky")'s label, Utopia, releasing the Julie Tippetts album, _Sunset Glow_. Tippett continued to play with various combinations of musicians through the 1970s, playing improvisational jazz and [jazz-rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz-rock "Jazz-rock") with such musicians as [Stan Tracey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stan_Tracey "Stan Tracey"), [Robert Wyatt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Wyatt "Robert Wyatt"), [Dudu Pukwana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dudu_Pukwana "Dudu Pukwana"), [Harry Miller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_Miller_(jazz_bassist) "Harry Miller (jazz bassist)"), Elton Dean, [Hugh Hopper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hugh_Hopper "Hugh Hopper"), and [Louis Moholo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_Moholo "Louis Moholo").[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Tippett#cite_note-guardian-1)[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Tippett#cite_note-Eder-2) From 1979, he also started to release many live albums of solo piano performances, beginning with _The Unlonely Raindancer_. In the late 1980s, he, along with [Paul Dunmall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Dunmall "Paul Dunmall") saxes, Paul Rogers bass, and [Tony Levin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Levin_(drummer) "Tony Levin (drummer)") drums, formed the quartet Mujician, playing purely improvised jazz.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Tippett#cite_note-LarkinJazz-4) Mujician released six albums between 1990 and 2002. He also formed a trio with Julie Tippetts and Willi Kellers, and wrote film and television scores. He also wrote music for [string quartets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/String_quartet "String quartet") and piano, and taught at summer schools. Tippett also continued to record and to tour in Britain and Europe with various ensembles. He also worked with musicians [Andy Sheppard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andy_Sheppard "Andy Sheppard"), as well as with his frequent collaborators Elton Dean, Louis Moholo, and Howard Riley.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Tippett#cite_note-Eder-2) [... middle omitted — see footer ...] | Videos | - _[Déjà Vrooom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/D%C3%A9j%C3%A0_Vrooom "Déjà Vrooom")_

(1977) | | | | _**The _Köln_ Concert**_ is a live solo double album by pianist [Keith Jarrett](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Jarrett "Keith Jarrett") recorded at the [Opera House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cologne_Opera#The_opera_house "Cologne Opera") in [Köln (Cologne)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cologne "Cologne"), [West Germany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Germany "West Germany"), on 24 January 1975 and released on [ECM Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ECM_Records "ECM Records") later that year.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_K%C3%B6ln_Concert#cite_note-ECM-1) It is the best-selling solo album in jazz history and the best-selling piano album. In 2025, the album was deemed "culturally, historically, or aesthetically significant" by the [Library of Congress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Library_of_Congress "Library of Congress") and selected for preservation in the [National Recording Registry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Recording_Registry "National Recording Registry").[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_K%C3%B6ln_Concert#cite_note-3) ## Concert and recording The concert was organized by 18-year-old [Vera Brandes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vera_Brandes "Vera Brandes"),[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_K%C3%B6ln_Concert#cite_note-Krueger_2015-4) then Germany's youngest concert promoter.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_K%C3%B6ln_Concert#cite_note-BBC_2011-5) The concert took place on a Friday at the late hour of 11:30 pm, following an earlier opera performance. The late time was the only one the administration would make available to Brandes for a jazz concert—the first at the Köln Opera House. The show was sold out, filled to capacity at over 1,400 people at a ticket price of 4 [DM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deutsche_Mark "Deutsche Mark"). At Jarrett's request, Brandes had selected a [Bösendorfer 290 Imperial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/B%C3%B6sendorfer_290_Imperial "Bösendorfer 290 Imperial") concert grand piano for the performance. However, there was some confusion by the opera house staff and instead they found another Bösendorfer piano backstage—a much smaller [baby grand piano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baby_grand_piano "Baby grand piano")—and, assuming it was the one requested, placed it on the stage. The error was discovered too late for the correct Bösendorfer to be delivered to the venue in time for the evening's concert. The piano they had was intended for rehearsals only and was in poor condition and required several hours of [tuning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piano_tuning "Piano tuning") and adjustment to make it playable.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_K%C3%B6ln_Concert#cite_note-B%C3%B6sendorfer_2010-6)[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_K%C3%B6ln_Concert#cite_note-Krueger_2015-4) The instrument was tinny and thin in the upper registers and weak in the bass register, and the pedals did not work properly.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_K%C3%B6ln_Concert#cite_note-Krueger_2015-4) While Brandes made an attempt and procured another grand piano up to Jarrett's standards to be delivered as an emergency, the piano tuner who had meanwhile arrived to fix the baby grand warned her that transporting a grand piano without the proper equipment at low temperatures in the middle of a rainstorm would irreparably damage the instrument, forcing Brandes to stick to the small one.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_K%C3%B6ln_Concert#cite_note-BBC_2011_Witness-7)[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_K%C3%B6ln_Concert#cite_note-Krueger_2015-4) Jarrett had performed a few days earlier in [Lausanne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solo_Concerts:_Bremen/Lausanne "Solo Concerts: Bremen/Lausanne"), Switzerland and although Brandes had sent him a ticket for a flight to Cologne on the record company's request, he exchanged the ticket for cash and joined ECM Records producer [Manfred Eicher](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manfred_Eicher "Manfred Eicher") travelling to Cologne by car in Eicher's old [Renault 4](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Renault_4 "Renault 4"), so they arrived at the opera house late in the afternoon tired after the exhaustingly long drive.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_K%C3%B6ln_Concert#cite_note-Krueger_2015-4) Jarrett had not slept well in several nights and was in pain from back problems, having to wear a [brace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Back_brace "Back brace") as a result. After trying out the substandard piano and learning a replacement instrument was not available, Jarrett nearly refused to play and was about to leave, but Brandes was able to convince him to perform anyway as the concert was scheduled to begin in just a few hours.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_K%C3%B6ln_Concert#cite_note-online.wsj.com-8)[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_K%C3%B6ln_Concert#cite_note-Krueger_2015-4) Brandes had booked a table at a restaurant in advance of the performance, but delays meant Jarrett was able to eat very little of the meal before leaving.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_K%C3%B6ln_Concert#cite_note-BBC_2011_Witness-7)[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_K%C3%B6ln_Concert#cite_note-Krueger_2015-4) Ultimately, Jarrett decided to play largely because the recording equipment was already set up.[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_K%C3%B6ln_Concert#cite_note-grammy-9) Jarrett used [ostinatos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ostinato "Ostinato") and rolling left-hand rhythmic figures during his performance to give the effect of stronger bass notes, and concentrated his playing in the middle portion of the keyboard. Eicher later said: "Probably \[Jarrett\] played it the way he did because it was not a good piano. Because he could not fall in love with the sound of it, he found another way to get the most out of it."[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_K%C3%B6ln_Concert#cite_note-online.wsj.com-8) A notable aspect of the concert was Jarrett's ability to produce very extensive improvised material over a [vamp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vamp_(music) "Vamp (music)") of one or two chords for prolonged periods of time. In Part I, he spends almost 12 minutes vamping over the chords Am7 (A minor 7) to G major, sometimes in a slow, [rubato](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rubato "Rubato") feel, and other times in a bluesy, gospel [rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rock_music "Rock music") feel. For about the last 6 minutes of Part I, he vamps over an A major theme. Roughly the first 8 minutes of Part II A is a vamp over a D major groove with a repeated bass vamp in the left hand, and in Part IIb, Jarrett improvises over an F♯ minor vamp for about the first 6 minutes. Originally dedicated to recording traditional jazz and small group swing, the label began to switch its attention to modern jazz around 1947. From there, Blue Note grew to become one of the most prolific, influential and respected jazz labels of the mid-20th century, noted for its role in facilitating the development of [hard bop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_bop "Hard bop"), [post-bop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post-bop "Post-bop") and [avant-garde jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avant-garde_jazz "Avant-garde jazz"), as well as for its iconic [modernist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modernism "Modernism") art direction. ## History \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Blue_Note_Records&action=edit§ion=1 "Edit section: History")\] Historically, Blue Note has principally been associated with the " [hard bop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_bop "Hard bop")" style of jazz (mixing [bebop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bebop "Bebop") with other forms of music including [soul](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soul_music "Soul music"), blues, [rhythm and blues](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhythm_and_blues "Rhythm and blues") and [gospel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gospel_music "Gospel music")), but also recorded essential albums in the [avant-garde](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avant-garde "Avant-garde") and [free](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_Jazz "Free Jazz") styles of jazz. [Horace Silver](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horace_Silver "Horace Silver"), [Jimmy Smith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jimmy_Smith_(musician) "Jimmy Smith (musician)"), [Freddie Hubbard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freddie_Hubbard "Freddie Hubbard"), [Lee Morgan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lee_Morgan "Lee Morgan"), [Art Blakey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_Blakey "Art Blakey"), [Grant Green](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grant_Green "Grant Green"), [Hank Mobley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hank_Mobley "Hank Mobley"), [Wayne Shorter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wayne_Shorter "Wayne Shorter"), [Bobby Hutcherson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bobby_Hutcherson "Bobby Hutcherson"), and [Jackie McLean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_McLean "Jackie McLean") were among the label's leading artists. During its heyday, the 1950s and 1960s, the photography and graphic art of [Reid Miles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reid_Miles "Reid Miles") created a series of iconic album covers, often incorporating session photos by [Francis Wolff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francis_Wolff "Francis Wolff"), which added to Blue Note's artistic reputation. ### Early years \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Blue_Note_Records&action=edit§ion=2 "Edit section: Early years")\] Lion first heard jazz as a young boy in [Berlin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berlin "Berlin"). He settled in [New York City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City "New York City") in 1937, and shortly after the first [From Spirituals to Swing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/From_Spirituals_to_Swing "From Spirituals to Swing") concert, recorded pianists [Albert Ammons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_Ammons "Albert Ammons") and [Meade Lux Lewis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meade_Lux_Lewis "Meade Lux Lewis") in 1939 during a one-day session in a rented studio.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Note_Records#cite_note-LarkinGE-2) The Blue Note label initially consisted of Lion and [Max Margulis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Max_Margulis "Max Margulis"), a communist writer who funded the project. The label's first releases were traditional "hot" jazz and [boogie woogie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boogie_woogie "Boogie woogie"), and the label's first hit was a performance of " [Summertime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Summertime_(George_Gershwin_song) "Summertime (George Gershwin song)")" by famous soprano saxophonist [Sidney Bechet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sidney_Bechet "Sidney Bechet"), which Bechet had been unable to record for the established companies.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Note_Records#cite_note-LarkinGE-2) Musicians were supplied with alcoholic refreshments, and recorded in the early hours of the morning after their evening's work in clubs and bars had finished. The label soon became known for treating musicians uncommonly well—setting up recording sessions at congenial times, and allowing the artists to be involved in all aspects of the record's production. Francis Wolff, a professional photographer, emigrated to the US at the end of 1939 and soon joined forces with Lion, a childhood friend.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Note_Records#cite_note-LarkinGE-2) In 1941, Lion was drafted into the army for two years. [Milt Gabler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milt_Gabler "Milt Gabler") at the [Commodore Music Store](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commodore_Records "Commodore Records") offered storage facilities and helped keep the catalog in print, with Wolff working for him. By late 1943, the label was back in business recording musicians and supplying records to the armed forces. Willing to record artists that most other labels would consider to be uncommercial, in December 1943 the label initiated more sessions with artists such as pianist [Art Hodes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_Hodes "Art Hodes"), trumpeter [Sidney De Paris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sidney_De_Paris "Sidney De Paris"), clarinetist [Edmond Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edmond_Hall "Edmond Hall"), and Harlem stride pianist [James P. Johnson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_P._Johnson "James P. Johnson"),[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Note_Records#cite_note-LarkinGE-2) who was returning to a high degree of musical activity after having largely recovered from a stroke suffered in 1940. ### Lion and Wolff embrace bebop \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Blue_Note_Records&action=edit§ion=3 "Edit section: Lion and Wolff embrace bebop")\] [... middle omitted — see footer ...] - # Contemporary Records Contemporary Records American record label Record label | Contemporary Records | | --- | | [![](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fc/Contemporary_Records_logo_1979.svg/500px-Contemporary_Records_logo_1979.svg.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Contemporary_Records_logo_1979.svg)
Logo used from 1979 to the mid-2000s | | Parent company | [Concord Bicycle Music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Concord_Bicycle_Music "Concord Bicycle Music") | | Founded | 1951(1951) | | Founder | [Lester Koenig](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lester_Koenig "Lester Koenig") | | Defunct | 1984(1984) | | Status | Inactive | | Genre | [Jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz "Jazz"), [West Coast jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Coast_jazz "West Coast jazz") | | Country of origin | U.S. | | Official website | [concord.com](http://www.concord.com//labels/contemporary) | **Contemporary Records** was a [jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz "Jazz") record company and label founded by [Lester Koenig](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lester_Koenig "Lester Koenig") in [Los Angeles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles "Los Angeles") in 1951. Contemporary produced music from a variety of jazz styles and players.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Contemporary_Records#cite_note-New_Grove-1) ## West Coast players Contemporary became identified with a style of jazz called [West Coast jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Coast_jazz "West Coast jazz") as exemplified by [Art Pepper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_Pepper "Art Pepper"), [Chet Baker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chet_Baker "Chet Baker"), [Shelly Manne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shelly_Manne "Shelly Manne"), and [André Previn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andr%C3%A9_Previn "André Previn").[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Contemporary_Records#cite_note-New_Grove-1) In the mid-1960s the company fell into relative limbo, but limited new recordings were made in the late 1970s, including a series of albums by Art Pepper recorded at the [Village Vanguard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Village_Vanguard "Village Vanguard") club in New York. After Les Koenig's death in 1977, the label was run for seven years by his son,[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Contemporary_Records#cite_note-New_Grove-1) John, who produced albums by [George Cables](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Cables "George Cables"), [Joe Farrell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Farrell "Joe Farrell"), [Joe Henderson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Henderson "Joe Henderson"), [Bobby Hutcherson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bobby_Hutcherson "Bobby Hutcherson"), [Peter Erskine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Erskine "Peter Erskine"), and [Chico Freeman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chico_Freeman "Chico Freeman"). In 1984 Contemporary was purchased by [Fantasy Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fantasy_Records "Fantasy Records"), which used the name for a short time. Most Contemporary titles were reissued by Fantasy. Also, some titles have found new life among today's audiophiles as high-quality LP [remasters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Audio_mastering "Audio mastering") from [Analogue Productions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Analogue_Productions "Analogue Productions") and other [audiophile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Audiophile "Audiophile") labels. The Fantasy catalog, including Contemporary and its associated labels, [Good Time Jazz Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Good_Time_Jazz_Records "Good Time Jazz Records"), Society for Forgotten Music, and Contemporary Composers Series, was sold to [Concord Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Concord_Records "Concord Records") in 2004. Over the years, a number of major figures in the music business worked for Contemporary. Among them were [Atlantic Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlantic_Records "Atlantic Records") executive [Nesuhi Ertegun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nesuhi_Ertegun "Nesuhi Ertegun"), writers [Nat Hentoff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nat_Hentoff "Nat Hentoff") and [Leonard Feather](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonard_Feather "Leonard Feather"), producer [Joe Boyd](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Boyd "Joe Boyd"), recording engineer and studio designer Howard Holzer, and mastering engineer [Bernie Grundman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bernie_Grundman "Bernie Grundman"). ## Recording Lester Koenig was very particular about high-fidelity sounds.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Contemporary_Records#cite_note-2) In 1956 Koenig hired away Roy DuNann from [Capitol Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capitol_Records "Capitol Records"), and DuNann provided some creative recording techniques for the label.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Contemporary_Records#cite_note-3) He said Koenig provided him with German ( [Neumann/Telefunken](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georg_Neumann "Georg Neumann") U-47) and Austrian ( [AKG](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AKG_Acoustics "AKG Acoustics") C-12) condenser microphones and he immediately noted the very high output of these microphones, especially close-in on jazz musicians' dynamic playing. DuNann achieved his signature sound—crisp, clear and balanced without distortion or unpleasant "peak presence"—by keeping his microphone setups very simple (generally one per musician) and avoided the use of pre-amplifiers for them. He built a simple passive mixing system that directly fed the electronics of his [Ampex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ampex#Audio_technology "Ampex") 350 and 351 tape machines. Also, DuNann told _Stereophile_ that Contemporary sessions were recorded "dry" (without electronic echo added or in a reverberant room). Sometimes, such as in the case of Sonny Rollins' _[Way Out West](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Way_Out_West_(Sonny_Rollins_album) "Way Out West (Sonny Rollins album)")_, a plate reverb unit was inserted between the tape machine and the [LP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LP_album "LP album") [disc cutting lathe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Disc_cutting_lathe "Disc cutting lathe"). This is why some later LP and [CD](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Compact_Disc "Compact Disc") reissues of Contemporary albums sound "dry" and "dead" compared to the original LPs mastered by DuNann. ## # Impulse! Records Impulse! Records American record label Record label | Impulse! Records | | --- | | [![](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/b/b1/Impulserecords.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Impulserecords.jpg) | | Parent company | [Universal Music Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universal_Music_Group "Universal Music Group") | | Founded | 1960(1960) | | Founder | [Creed Taylor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Creed_Taylor "Creed Taylor") | | Distributor | [Verve Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Verve_Records "Verve Records") | | Genre | [Jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz "Jazz") | | Country of origin | U.S. | | Location | [New York, New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York,_New_York "New York, New York") | | Official website | [www.impulserecords.com](http://www.impulserecords.com/) | **Impulse! Records** (occasionally styled as "¡mpulse! Records" and "¡!") is an American [jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz "Jazz") [record label](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Record_label "Record label") established by [Creed Taylor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Creed_Taylor "Creed Taylor") in 1960. [John Coltrane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Coltrane "John Coltrane") was among Impulse!'s earliest signings. Thanks to consistent sales and positive critiques of his recordings, the label came to be known as "the house that Trane built".[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impulse!_Records#cite_note-1) ## History Impulse!'s parent company, [ABC-Paramount Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ABC-Paramount_Records "ABC-Paramount Records"), was established in 1955 as the recording division of the American Broadcasting Company ( [ABC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Broadcasting_Company "American Broadcasting Company")). In the 1940s and 1950s, ABC benefitted from the U.S. government's [antitrust](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antitrust "Antitrust") actions against broadcasters and film studios who were forced to divest parts of their companies. In the early 1950s, ABC acquired the [Blue Network](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Network "Blue Network") of radio stations from [NBC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NBC "NBC") and later merged with the newly independent Paramount Theaters chain, formerly owned by [Paramount Pictures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paramount_Pictures "Paramount Pictures"). The new recording division was located at [1501 Broadway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1501_Broadway "1501 Broadway"), above the [Paramount Theatre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paramount_Theatre_(New_York_City) "Paramount Theatre (New York City)") in [Times Square](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Square "Times Square").[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impulse!_Records#cite_note-2) Under the leadership of [Leonard Goldenson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonard_Goldenson "Leonard Goldenson"), the former head of Paramount Pictures, the company "sought to establish itself as a cross-media force in television, theaters and sound recordings".[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impulse!_Records#cite_note-3) It enjoyed early success in TV with _[The Mickey Mouse Club](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Mickey_Mouse_Club "The Mickey Mouse Club")_, a joint venture with [Disney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Disney "Disney"). To market music from the successful TV show, ABC-Paramount established the Am-Par Record Corporation and the ABC-Paramount label in early 1955, appointing Sam Clark, a Boston record distributor, as president, with Larry Newton as sales manager and Harry Levine the A&R director. The new recording company enjoyed Goldenson's full support. Sid Feller, a producer and arranger, was the first salaried employee on July 15, 1955.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impulse!_Records#cite_note-4) The label achieved early success in [pop music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pop_music "Pop music") with [Paul Anka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Anka "Paul Anka"). A young producer named [Creed Taylor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Creed_Taylor "Creed Taylor"), who also worked for a period at [Bethlehem Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bethlehem_Records "Bethlehem Records") in 1955, produced some of ABC-Paramount/Am-Par's earliest albums for musicians such as [Urbie Green](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Urbie_Green "Urbie Green"), [Billy Taylor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billy_Taylor "Billy Taylor"), [Oscar Pettiford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oscar_Pettiford "Oscar Pettiford"), [Kenny Dorham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenny_Dorham "Kenny Dorham") and [Zoot Sims](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zoot_Sims "Zoot Sims"). In 1960, Am-Par established a jazz subsidiary and hired Taylor as producer and A&R manager. He chose the name "Pulse" but then learned there was already a label with that name, so he added a prefix. In the mid-1960s, the headquarters of Impulse! was moved to 1130 [Avenue of the Americas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avenue_of_the_Americas "Avenue of the Americas").[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impulse!_Records#cite_note-5) ### Design Impulse!'s albums are known for their visual appeal. The black, orange, and white [livery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Livery "Livery") was devised by [Fran Attaway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fran_Attaway?action=edit&redlink=1 "Fran Attaway") (then known as Fran Scott), whom Taylor also credits with establishing the label's tradition of using cutting-edge photographers for its covers.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impulse!_Records#cite_note-6) The color scheme was chosen for its brightness and because no other label used this combination.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impulse!_Records#cite_note-7) The label's logo featured the Impulse! name in a heavy, sans-serif, lower-cased font, followed by an exclamation mark that mirrors the lower-case "i" at the beginning. For most of the 1960s, Impulse!'s album covers featured the logo in orange letters in a white circle, with black-and-orange exclamation marks above it, and the catalog number below it. One exception is the album _[A Love Supreme](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_Love_Supreme "A Love Supreme")_, which used the design in black and white. In 1968 the circular front-cover badge was replaced by a one-color design featuring a simplified Impulse! logo and the ABC Records logo side by side within a divided rectangular border. Album covers often featured stylish, large-format photographs or paintings, usually in color, which were typically bled out to the edges of the cover and printed on glossy laminated stock. Many of the best-known Impulse! covers were designed by art director [Robert Flynn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Flynn_(graphic_designer)?action=edit&redlink=1 "Robert Flynn (graphic designer)") and photographed by a small group that included [Pete Turner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Turner_(photographer) "Pete Turner (photographer)"), who shot covers for Verve, [A&M](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A&M_Records "A&M Records"), and [CTI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CTI_Records "CTI Records"); [Chuck Stewart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chuck_Stewart "Chuck Stewart"); [Arnold Newman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arnold_Newman "Arnold Newman"); [Ted Russell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ted_Russell_(photographer)?action=edit&redlink=1 "Ted Russell (photographer)"); and [Joe Alper](https://web.archive.org/web/20090323120015/http://www.bobdylanphotobook.com/), who was known for his early ’60s photographs of [Bob Dylan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Dylan "Bob Dylan")) The sparse black-and-white back covers bore the slogan "The New Wave of Jazz is on IMPULSE!" Most Impulse! LPs were issued in a gatefold sleeve, with photographs, liner notes, and, in some cases, multi-page booklets. ### Early success Taylor achieved early success by signing [Ray Charles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ray_Charles "Ray Charles"), who had just ended his contract with [Atlantic Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlantic_Records "Atlantic Records"). Charles's _[Genius + Soul = Jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genius_+_Soul_=_Jazz "Genius + Soul = Jazz")_ gave the label its first hit and became the fourth-highest charting album of his career.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impulse!_Records#cite_note-8) Other early successes included _[Out of the Cool](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Out_of_the_Cool "Out of the Cool")_ by [Gil Evans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gil_Evans "Gil Evans"). A major proponent of collective [improvisation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_improvisation "Jazz improvisation"), he is considered one of the greatest jazz musicians and composers in history,[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Mingus#cite_note-Underdog-1) with a career spanning three decades and collaborations with other jazz greats, such as [Duke Ellington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duke_Ellington "Duke Ellington"), [Charlie Parker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charlie_Parker "Charlie Parker"), [Max Roach](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Max_Roach "Max Roach"), and [Eric Dolphy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Dolphy "Eric Dolphy"). Mingus's work ranged from advanced [bebop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bebop "Bebop") and [avant-garde jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avant-garde_jazz "Avant-garde jazz") with small and midsize [ensembles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_band "Jazz band") to pioneering the [post-bop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post-bop "Post-bop") style on seminal recordings like _[Pithecanthropus Erectus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pithecanthropus_Erectus_(album) "Pithecanthropus Erectus (album)")_ (1956) and _[Mingus Ah Um](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mingus_Ah_Um "Mingus Ah Um")_ (1959) and [progressive big band](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_music#Jazz "Progressive music") experiments such as _[The Black Saint and the Sinner Lady](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Black_Saint_and_the_Sinner_Lady "The Black Saint and the Sinner Lady")_ (1963). Mingus's compositions continue to be played by contemporary musicians ranging from the repertory bands [Mingus Big Band](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mingus_Big_Band "Mingus Big Band"), [Mingus Dynasty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mingus_Dynasty_(band) "Mingus Dynasty (band)"), and Mingus Orchestra to high school students who play the charts and compete in the Charles Mingus High School Competition.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Mingus#cite_note-2) In 1993, the [Library of Congress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Library_of_Congress "Library of Congress") acquired Mingus's collected papers—including scores, sound recordings, correspondence, and photos—in what it called "the most important acquisition of a manuscript collection relating to jazz in the Library's history".[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Mingus#cite_note-3) ## Biography ### Early life and career Mingus was born in [Nogales, Arizona](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nogales,_Arizona "Nogales, Arizona"), in 1922, to Charles Mingus Sr., a staff sergeant in the [U.S. Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Army "United States Army"), and Harriet Sophia Mingus (née Phillips). His family moved to the [Watts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Watts,_Los_Angeles "Watts, Los Angeles") area of Los Angeles shortly after his birth.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Mingus#cite_note-FOOTNOTESantoro2000b13%E2%80%9314-4) Charles Sr. was born in 1877 in [Swain County, North Carolina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swain_County,_North_Carolina "Swain County, North Carolina"), in the [Great Smoky Mountains](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Smoky_Mountains "Great Smoky Mountains"). His mother was a white teenager, Clarinda Mingus; his father was Daniel Mingus, a farmhand and former slave who worked for Clarinda's family. Clarinda married and started a new family when he was six, leaving him in the care of her father and grandparents.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Mingus#cite_note-5) He left home at fourteen, enlisting in the army and seeing action in the [Spanish–American War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish%E2%80%93American_War "Spanish–American War"). In 1917, he married Harriet Sophia Phillips, who was of mixed Chinese and African-American descent. She died of [myocarditis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Myocarditis "Myocarditis") in 1922, a few months after the birth of their son.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Mingus#cite_note-FOOTNOTESantoro2000b14%E2%80%9317-6) Mingus was raised alongside his two elder half-sisters, from his father's first marriage. His father was married for a third time in 1923, to Mamie Carson.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Mingus#cite_note-FOOTNOTESantoro2000b18-7) Mamie allowed only [church-related music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Church_music "Church music") in their home, but Mingus developed an early love for other music, especially that of [Duke Ellington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duke_Ellington "Duke Ellington"). He studied [trombone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trombone "Trombone"), and later [cello](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cello "Cello"), although he was unable to follow the cello professionally because, at the time, it was nearly impossible for a black musician to make a career of [classical music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Classical_music "Classical music"), and the cello was not accepted as a jazz instrument. Despite this, Mingus remained attached to the cello; as he studied bass with [Red Callender](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_Callender "Red Callender") in the late 1930s, Callender even commented that the cello was still Mingus's main instrument. In his autobiography, _Beneath the Underdog_, Mingus states that he did not actually start learning bass until [Buddy Collette](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buddy_Collette "Buddy Collette") accepted him into his swing band under the stipulation that he be the band's bass player.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Mingus#cite_note-autogenerated1991-8) Due to a poor education, the young Mingus could not read musical notation quickly enough to join the local youth orchestra. This had a serious impact on his early musical experiences, leaving him feeling ostracized from the classical music world. These early experiences, in addition to his lifelong confrontations with racism, were reflected in his music, which often focused on themes of racism, discrimination, and (in)justice.[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Mingus#cite_note-Horton-9) [... middle omitted — see footer ...] | --- | | International | - [ISNI](https://isni.org/isni/0000000110832626)

[Jump to content](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Coltrane_discography#bodyContent) From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia | [John Coltrane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Coltrane "John Coltrane") discography | | --- | | [![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/66/John_Coltrane_1963.jpg/250px-John_Coltrane_1963.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:John_Coltrane_1963.jpg)
John Coltrane in 1963 | | Studio albums | 45 | | Live albums | 11 | | Compilation albums | 23 | | Singles | 19 | | Video albums | 2 | | Appearances | 59 | | Documentaries | 3 | | Television | 2 | This article presents the [discography](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discography "Discography") of the American [jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz "Jazz") [saxophonist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saxophone "Saxophone") and [bandleader](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bandleader "Bandleader") [John Coltrane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Coltrane "John Coltrane") (1926–1967). ## Introduction \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=John_Coltrane_discography&action=edit§ion=1 "Edit section: Introduction")\] Coltrane participated in his first recording sessions while enlisted in the Navy from August 6, 1945, to August 11, 1946.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Coltrane_discography#cite_note-1) He performed eight numbers in a pickup band that included trumpeter Dexter Culbertson.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Coltrane_discography#cite_note-2) These were private recordings not made for official release. However, one track from the session, " [Hot House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hot_House_(composition) "Hot House (composition)")", eventually appeared on the 1992 compilation _[The Last Giant: The John Coltrane Anthology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Last_Giant:_Anthology "The Last Giant: Anthology")._[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Coltrane_discography#cite_note-3) There are conflicting sources as to whether he made his first professional recording session with [Dinah Washington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dinah_Washington "Dinah Washington"): Jazzdisco.org[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Coltrane_discography#cite_note-4) lists the session as September 27, 1949 in New York City, but Lewis Porter's _John Coltrane: His Life and Music_ states that he was on tour with the [Dizzy Gillespie Big Band](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dizzy_Gillespie "Dizzy Gillespie") during that time.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Coltrane_discography#cite_note-5) Most sources confirm that he recorded with Billy Valentine on November 7 in Los Angeles for [Mercury Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mercury_Records "Mercury Records"). In subsequent years, Coltrane sat in on recording sessions with Gillespie, [Johnny Hodges](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johnny_Hodges "Johnny Hodges"), [Earl Bostic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earl_Bostic "Earl Bostic"), and Gay Crosse. In September 1955, Coltrane joined the [Miles Davis Quintet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis_Quintet "Miles Davis Quintet")[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Coltrane_discography#cite_note-6) and appeared on several [Miles Davis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis "Miles Davis")-led recordings, including _['Round About Midnight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/'Round_About_Midnight "'Round About Midnight")_ and _[Milestones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milestones_(Miles_Davis_album) "Milestones (Miles Davis album)")_. He briefly joined [Thelonious Monk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thelonious_Monk "Thelonious Monk") in May 1957, and their handful of recordings together have been collected on albums such as 1961's _[Thelonious Monk with John Coltrane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thelonious_Monk_with_John_Coltrane "Thelonious Monk with John Coltrane")_. In 1958, he rejoined Davis' band and stayed until April 1960; during that time he participated in the 1959 _[Kind of Blue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kind_of_Blue "Kind of Blue")_ sessions. In April 1957, he signed a contract with [Prestige Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prestige_Records "Prestige Records"); it is unclear if this was a two-year deal or a one-year contract plus a one-year option.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Coltrane_discography#cite_note-7)[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Coltrane_discography#cite_note-8) Many of Coltrane's recordings for Prestige could be classified as "sideman" recordings and informal [jam sessions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jam_sessions "Jam sessions") (or "blowing sessions", in the then-current terminology). He also made his first albums as a group leader, including his 1957 debut, _[Coltrane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coltrane_(1957_album) "Coltrane (1957 album)")_. That same year, Prestige allowed him to fulfill a promise that he would make an album for [Blue Note](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Note_Records "Blue Note Records"),[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Coltrane_discography#cite_note-9) leading to 1958's _[Blue Train](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Train_(album) "Blue Train (album)")_. After Coltrane gained prominence in the early 1960s, Prestige reissued a number of Coltrane's sideman and jam sessions under his name to capitalize on his success. _[The Prestige Recordings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Complete_Prestige_Recordings_(John_Coltrane_album) "The Complete Prestige Recordings (John Coltrane album)")_ collects all of Coltrane's recordings for Prestige with the exception of his sideman work with Davis. When his Prestige contract expired, Coltrane signed a two-year contract (one year, plus a one-year option) with [Atlantic Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlantic_Records "Atlantic Records") in April 1959.[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Coltrane_discography#cite_note-10)[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Coltrane_discography#cite_note-11) He was the leader of all of these sessions except _[Bags & Trane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bags_&_Trane "Bags & Trane")_ and _[The Avant-Garde](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Avant-Garde_(album) "The Avant-Garde (album)")_, where he was featured with [Milt Jackson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milt_Jackson "Milt Jackson") and [Don Cherry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter) "Don Cherry (trumpeter)") respectively. Albums from this period include _[Giant Steps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giant_Steps "Giant Steps")_ and _[My Favorite Things](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/My_Favorite_Things_(John_Coltrane_album) "My Favorite Things (John Coltrane album)")_. The _[Heavyweight Champion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heavyweight_Champion:_The_Complete_Atlantic_Recordings_(album) "Heavyweight Champion: The Complete Atlantic Recordings (album)")_ box collects his recordings for Atlantic, including all known outtakes. Coltrane became the first artist to sign with the new [Impulse! Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impulse!_Records "Impulse! Records") when it bought out his Atlantic contract in April 1961.[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Coltrane_discography#cite_note-12) He would record for the label until the end of his life, and his success earned Impulse! a reputation as "The House That Trane Built".[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Coltrane_discography#cite_note-13) Albums from this final period include the live album _[Live at Birdland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Live_at_Birdland_(1964_John_Coltrane_album) "Live at Birdland (1964 John Coltrane album)")_, _[A Love Supreme](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_Love_Supreme "A Love Supreme")_, and _[Ascension](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ascension_(John_Coltrane_album) "Ascension (John Coltrane album)")_. All of the companies Coltrane worked with during his lifetime have compiled and reissued his material. In addition, Impulse! has issued several previously unreleased live recordings, including _[Live in Japan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Live_in_Japan_(John_Coltrane_album) "Live in Japan (John Coltrane album)")_ and _[The Olatunji Concert: The Last Live Recording](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olatunji_Concert "Olatunji Concert")_. Coltrane's concert, television and radio performances generated dozens of unauthorized and [bootleg recordings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bootleg_recording "Bootleg recording"). [Pablo Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pablo_Records "Pablo Records"), a label that specializes in live recordings,[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Coltrane_discography#cite_note-14) purchased rights to several tapes of his performances,[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Coltrane_discography#cite_note-15) and is therefore considered a legitimate source despite never signing him to its label. ## Studio albums [... middle omitted — see footer ...] | Related | - [List of sessions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_John_Coltrane_recording_sessions "List of John Coltrane recording sessions")
