- [acoustic guitar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Acoustic_guitar "Acoustic guitar") | **Modal jazz** is [jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz "Jazz") that makes use of [musical modes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mode_(music) "Mode (music)"), often [modulating](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modulation_(music) "Modulation (music)") among them to accompany the [chords](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chord_(music) "Chord (music)") instead of relying on one [tonal center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tonic_(music) "Tonic (music)") used across the piece. Though exerting influence to the present, modal jazz was most popular in the 1950s and 1960s, as evidenced by the success of [Miles Davis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis "Miles Davis")'s 1958 composition " [Milestones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milestones_(composition) "Milestones (composition)")" and 1959 album _[Kind of Blue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kind_of_Blue "Kind of Blue")_, and [John Coltrane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Coltrane "John Coltrane")'s quartet from 1960 to 1965. Other performers of modal jazz include [Chick Corea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chick_Corea "Chick Corea"), [Bill Evans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans "Bill Evans"), [Herbie Hancock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbie_Hancock "Herbie Hancock"), [Joe Henderson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Henderson "Joe Henderson"), [Bobby Hutcherson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bobby_Hutcherson "Bobby Hutcherson"), [Pharoah Sanders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pharoah_Sanders "Pharoah Sanders"), [Woody Shaw](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Woody_Shaw "Woody Shaw"), [Wayne Shorter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wayne_Shorter "Wayne Shorter"), [McCoy Tyner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/McCoy_Tyner "McCoy Tyner"), and [Larry Young](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Larry_Young_(musician) "Larry Young (musician)").[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modal_jazz#cite_note-Essential-1) ## History In [bebop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bebop "Bebop") as well as in [hard bop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_bop "Hard bop"), musicians use chords to provide the background for solos. A piece starts out with a theme that introduces a series of chords for the solos. These chords repeat throughout the whole piece, while the soloists play new, improvised themes over the repeated [chord progression](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chord_progression "Chord progression"). By the 1950s, improvising over chords had become such a dominant part of jazz that sidemen at recording dates were sometimes given nothing more than a list of chords to play from.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modal_jazz#cite_note-2) [Mercer Ellington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mercer_Ellington "Mercer Ellington") has stated that [Juan Tizol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juan_Tizol "Juan Tizol") conceived the melody to " [Caravan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caravan_(1937_song) "Caravan (1937 song)")" in 1936 as a result of his days studying music in Puerto Rico, where they could not afford much sheet music so the teacher would turn the music upside down after they had learned to play it right-side up.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modal_jazz#cite_note-mercer1994-3) This "inversion" technique led to a modal sound throughout Tizol's work.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modal_jazz#cite_note-mercer1994-3) [Sun Ra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sun_Ra "Sun Ra") reportedly rehearsed a small group consisting of [Harold Ousley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harold_Ousley "Harold Ousley"), [Vernel Fournier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vernel_Fournier "Vernel Fournier"), and [Wilbur Ware](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilbur_Ware "Wilbur Ware") in 1950 that played original songs that were modal in which the melody was based on a single chord or [vamp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ostinato#Vamp "Ostinato") – ten years before this approach became popular in jazz.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modal_jazz#cite_note-4) Saxophonist [Wayne Shorter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wayne_Shorter "Wayne Shorter") has noted that the 1953 composition " [Glass Enclosure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glass_Enclosure "Glass Enclosure")" by pianist Bud Powell was one of the earliest jazz compositions to make use of [Lydian chords](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lydian_chord "Lydian chord"), based on the [Lydian mode](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lydian_mode "Lydian mode") that was not widely used in jazz until about a decade later.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modal_jazz#cite_note-5) Powell's 1951 [Un Poco Loco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Un_Poco_Loco "Un Poco Loco") uses the Lydian chords and even uses Lydian chords stacked on top of each implying a [polytonality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polytonality "Polytonality") (D [major 7](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Major_seventh_chord "Major seventh chord") over C major 7: CEGBDF#AC#) with the improvisation based on alternating Lydian-ish polytonality and an [altered dominant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Altered_dominant "Altered dominant") chord.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modal_jazz#cite_note-6) Towards the end of the 1950s, spurred by the experiments of composer and bandleader George Russell, musicians began using a modal approach. They chose not to write their pieces using conventional chord changes, but instead using modes. Musicians employing this technique include Miles Davis, [Freddie Hubbard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freddie_Hubbard "Freddie Hubbard"), Bill Evans, [Herbie Hancock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbie_Hancock "Herbie Hancock"), and Wayne Shorter. (m.1954;div.1964)​ | Musical artist **Randolph Denard Ornette Coleman** (March 9, 1930 – June 11, 2015)[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornette_Coleman#cite_note-Ratliff-1) was an American [jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz "Jazz") saxophonist, trumpeter, violinist, and composer. He is best known as a principal founder of the [free jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_jazz "Free jazz") genre, a term derived from his 1960 album _[Free Jazz: A Collective Improvisation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_Jazz:_A_Collective_Improvisation "Free Jazz: A Collective Improvisation")_. His pioneering works often abandoned the [harmony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harmony "Harmony")-based composition, [tonality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tonality "Tonality"), chord changes, and fixed rhythm found in earlier jazz idioms;[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornette_Coleman#cite_note-2) instead, Coleman emphasized an experimental approach to [improvisation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Improvisation "Improvisation") rooted in ensemble playing and [blues](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blues "Blues") phrasing.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornette_Coleman#cite_note-allmusicbio-3) Thom Jurek of [AllMusic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AllMusic "AllMusic") called him "one of the most beloved and polarizing figures in jazz history", noting that while "now celebrated as a fearless innovator and a genius, he was initially regarded by peers and critics as rebellious, disruptive, and even a fraud."[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornette_Coleman#cite_note-allmusicbio-3) Born and raised in [Fort Worth, Texas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Worth,_Texas "Fort Worth, Texas"), Coleman taught himself to play the saxophone when he was a teenager.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornette_Coleman#cite_note-Ratliff-1) He began his musical career playing in local [R&B](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhythm_and_blues "Rhythm and blues") and [bebop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bebop "Bebop") groups and eventually formed his own jazz group in [Los Angeles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles "Los Angeles"), featuring members such as [Ed Blackwell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Blackwell "Ed Blackwell"), [Don Cherry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter) "Don Cherry (trumpeter)"), [Charlie Haden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charlie_Haden "Charlie Haden"), and [Billy Higgins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billy_Higgins "Billy Higgins"). In November 1959, his quartet began a controversial residency at the [Five Spot Café](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Five_Spot_Caf%C3%A9 "Five Spot Café") in New York City and he released the influential album _[The Shape of Jazz to Come](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Shape_of_Jazz_to_Come "The Shape of Jazz to Come")_ on [Atlantic Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlantic_Records "Atlantic Records"). Coleman's subsequent Atlantic releases in the early 1960s would profoundly impact the direction of jazz in that decade, and his compositions " [Lonely Woman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lonely_Woman_(composition) "Lonely Woman (composition)")" and " [Broadway Blues](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Broadway_Blues_(Coleman) "Broadway Blues (Coleman)")" became [standards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_standard "Jazz standard") cited as important early works in free jazz.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornette_Coleman#cite_note-HellmerLawn2005-4) In the mid 1960s, Coleman left Atlantic for other labels, including [Blue Note](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Note_Records "Blue Note Records") and [Columbia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbia_Records "Columbia Records"), and began performing with his young son [Denardo Coleman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denardo_Coleman "Denardo Coleman") on drums. He explored symphonic composition with his 1972 album _[Skies of America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skies_of_America "Skies of America")_, featuring the [London Symphony Orchestra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Symphony_Orchestra "London Symphony Orchestra"). In the mid-1970s, he formed the group [Prime Time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prime_Time_(band) "Prime Time (band)"), which performed electric [jazz-funk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz-funk "Jazz-funk") and elaborated on his theory of [harmolodics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harmolodics "Harmolodics").[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornette_Coleman#cite_note-allmusicbio-3) In 1995, he and Denardo founded the [Harmolodic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harmolodics#Record_label "Harmolodics") record label. Coleman's 2006 album _[Sound Grammar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sound_Grammar "Sound Grammar")_ received the 2007 [Pulitzer Prize for Music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pulitzer_Prize_for_Music "Pulitzer Prize for Music"), making him the second jazz musician ever to receive the honor.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornette_Coleman#cite_note-5) ## Biography \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ornette_Coleman&action=edit§ion=1 "Edit section: Biography")\] ### Early life \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ornette_Coleman&action=edit§ion=2 "Edit section: Early life")\] Coleman was born Randolph Denard Ornette Coleman on March 9, 1930, in [Fort Worth, Texas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Worth,_Texas "Fort Worth, Texas"),[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornette_Coleman#cite_note-Fordham-6) where he was raised.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornette_Coleman#cite_note-Atlantic1972-7)[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornette_Coleman#cite_note-EGP-8)[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornette_Coleman#cite_note-Litweiler-9) He attended [I.M. Terrell High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/I.M._Terrell_High_School "I.M. Terrell High School") in Fort Worth, where he participated in the band program until he was dismissed for improvising during [John Philip Sousa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Philip_Sousa "John Philip Sousa")'s march " [The Washington Post](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Washington_Post_(march) "The Washington Post (march)")". He began performing [R&B](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhythm_and_blues "Rhythm and blues") and [bebop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bebop "Bebop") on tenor saxophone, and formed The Jam Jivers with [Prince Lasha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_Lasha "Prince Lasha") and [Charles Moffett](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Moffett "Charles Moffett").[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornette_Coleman#cite_note-Litweiler-9) [... middle omitted — see footer ...] - His music is characterized by an energetic, physical approach, resulting in complex [improvisation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Musical_improvisation "Musical improvisation") often involving [tone clusters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tone_clusters "Tone clusters") and intricate [polyrhythms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polyrhythms "Polyrhythms"). His technique has been compared to [percussion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Percussion_instrument "Percussion instrument"). Referring to the number of keys on a standard piano, [Val Wilmer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Val_Wilmer "Val Wilmer") used the phrase "eighty-eight tuned drums" to describe Taylor's style.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_Taylor#cite_note-6) He has been referred to as " [Art Tatum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_Tatum "Art Tatum") with contemporary-classical leanings".[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_Taylor#cite_note-Tatum-7) ## Early life and education \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Cecil_Taylor&action=edit§ion=1 "Edit section: Early life and education")\] Cecil Percival Taylor was born on March 25, 1929, in [Long Island City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Long_Island_City "Long Island City"), [Queens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Queens "Queens"),[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_Taylor#cite_note-nytobit-8) and raised in [Corona, Queens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corona,_Queens "Corona, Queens").[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_Taylor#cite_note-NYT2012-9) As an only child in a middle-class family, Taylor was encouraged by his mother, Almeda Ragland Taylor, to play music at an early age. He began playing piano at age six and went on to study at the [New York College of Music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_College_of_Music "New York College of Music") and [New England Conservatory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_England_Conservatory "New England Conservatory") in [Boston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston "Boston"). At the New England Conservatory, Taylor majored in popular music arrangement. During his time there, he also became familiar with contemporary European [art music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_music "Art music"). [Bela Bartók](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/B%C3%A9la_Bart%C3%B3k "Béla Bartók") and [Karlheinz Stockhausen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karlheinz_Stockhausen "Karlheinz Stockhausen") notably influenced his music.[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_Taylor#cite_note-:0-10) In 1955, Taylor moved back to New York City from Boston. He formed a quartet with soprano saxophonist [Steve Lacy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_Lacy_(saxophonist) "Steve Lacy (saxophonist)"), bassist [Buell Neidlinger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buell_Neidlinger "Buell Neidlinger"), and drummer [Dennis Charles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denis_Charles "Denis Charles").[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_Taylor#cite_note-:0-10) Taylor's first recording, _[Jazz Advance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_Advance "Jazz Advance")_, featured Lacy and was released in 1956.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_Taylor#cite_note-11) The recording is described by [Richard Cook](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Cook_(journalist) "Richard Cook (journalist)") and [Brian Morton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brian_Morton_(Scottish_writer) "Brian Morton (Scottish writer)") in the _[Penguin Guide to Jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Penguin_Guide_to_Jazz "Penguin Guide to Jazz")_: "While there are still many nods to conventional [post-bop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post-bop "Post-bop") form in this set, it already points to the freedoms in which the pianist would later immerse himself."[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_Taylor#cite_note-12) Taylor's quartet featuring Lacy also appeared at the 1957 [Newport Jazz Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newport_Jazz_Festival "Newport Jazz Festival"), which was made into the album _[At Newport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/At_Newport_(Cecil_Taylor_and_Gigi_Gryce_album) "At Newport (Cecil Taylor and Gigi Gryce album)")_.[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_Taylor#cite_note-13) Taylor collaborated with saxophonist [John Coltrane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Coltrane "John Coltrane") in 1958 on _[Stereo Drive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stereo_Drive "Stereo Drive")_, now available as _Coltrane Time_.[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_Taylor#cite_note-14) ## 1950s and early 1960s \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Cecil_Taylor&action=edit§ion=2 "Edit section: 1950s and early 1960s")\] Throughout the 1950s and 1960s, Taylor's music grew more complex and moved away from existing jazz styles. Gigs were often hard to come by, and club owners found that Taylor's approach of playing long pieces tended to impede business.[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_Taylor#cite_note-15) His 1959 [LP record](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LP_record "LP record") _[Looking Ahead!](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Looking_Ahead! "Looking Ahead!")_ showcased his innovation as a creator as compared to the jazz mainstream. Unlike others at the time, Taylor utilized virtuosic techniques and made swift stylistic shifts from phrase to phrase. These qualities, among others, still remained notable distinctions of his music for the rest of his life.[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_Taylor#cite_note-16) [... middle omitted — see footer ...] - "M-Base-concept" is short for " **m** acro **-b** asic **a** rray of **s** tructured **e** xtemporization", and critics have used this term to categorize this scene's music as a style of [jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz "Jazz").[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M-Base#cite_note-1) But Coleman stressed "M-Base" doesn't denote a musical style but a way of thinking about creating music.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M-Base#cite_note-2) However, Coleman has expressed discomfort with the term “jazz” to describe his music and also says M-Base was intended to be more expansive than describing music alone. M-Base was associated with a loose collective of young African American musicians and other performers active in and around [Brooklyn, New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brooklyn,_New_York "Brooklyn, New York"). The M-Base collective included Coleman, [Graham Haynes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graham_Haynes "Graham Haynes"), [Cassandra Wilson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cassandra_Wilson "Cassandra Wilson"), [Geri Allen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geri_Allen "Geri Allen"), [Robin Eubanks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robin_Eubanks "Robin Eubanks"), and [Greg Osby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greg_Osby "Greg Osby"). However, the musicians of the M-Base movement, which also included dancers and poets, strived for common creative musical languages, so their early recordings show many similarities reflecting their common ideas, the experiences of working together, and their similar cultural background. To label this kind of music, jazz critics have established the word "M-Base" as a jazz style for lack of a better term, distorting its original meaning.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M-Base#cite_note-3) ## Music associated with the term "M-Base" \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=M-Base&action=edit§ion=1 "Edit section: Music associated with the term \"M-Base\"")\] In 1991 a significant number of M-Base participants labelled as "M-Base Collective" recorded the CD _Anatomy of a Groove_. Most of them previously contributed to CDs by alto saxophonist Steve Coleman, whose creativity has been a pivotal factor in that movement,[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M-Base#cite_note-4) although he refused to be called its leader or founder. Coleman and his friend Greg Osby, who plays alto saxophone in a related style, together led the group Strata Institute, which recorded two CDs (the second with tenor saxophonist Von Freeman as a further leader). Under the name of Osby, a number of CDs with a specific character have been released starting in 1987, which also coined the perception of "M-Base" jazz. Tenor saxophonist and flutist Gary Thomas admittedly didn't take part in the M-Base initiative, but joined them, and there were similarities in his way of playing. He can be heard on recordings of Coleman and Osby, and his own CDs are also labelled as "M-Base-style". All three saxophonists contributed to the CD _[Jumpworld](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jumpworld "Jumpworld")_ by singer Cassandra Wilson. Pianist [Andrew Hill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Hill_(jazz_musician) "Andrew Hill (jazz musician)") said about Greg Osby: "He has an incredible sense of rhythm and harmonic accuracy, and picks the right notes with a precision that isn't common to people with his technical versatility. He's developed into a fully rounded artist who can play various styles extremely well – better than most."[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M-Base#cite_note-5) Greg Osby said about [Gary Thomas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gary_Thomas_(musician) "Gary Thomas (musician)"): "He's extremely intelligent and has a capacity for absorption that exceeds that of most people that I know \[…\] He has his own compositional and improvisational method that is peerless in my opinion. He's my favourite tenor saxophone player on the contemporary scene."[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M-Base#cite_note-6) Clarinettist and composer Don Byron called Steve Coleman "an exceptional personality of American music history."[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M-Base#cite_note-7) [... middle omitted — see footer ...] | **[![icon](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/53/Saxo_Boca1.JPG/20px-Saxo_Boca1.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Saxo_Boca1.JPG)[Jazzportal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portal:Jazz "Portal:Jazz")** | Retrieved from " [https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=M-Base&oldid=1359553569](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=M-Base&oldid=1359553569)" [Category](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:Category "Help:Category"): -
